title: Song of Solomon 1:1–7
context: The Song opens with a title calling it the Song of songs, a Hebrew way of saying the finest of songs, and linking it to Solomon (compare 1 Kings 4:32). The phrase which is Solomon’s can mean by, for, or about Solomon, so authorship and date are debated, and interpreters hold the question with varying confidence. The WEB divides the poetry among speakers it labels Beloved, Lover, and Friends; the Hebrew text does not mark speakers, so these labels are interpretive aids, and attributions vary at points. In these verses the WEB assigns most lines to the Beloved, who longs for the one she loves, delights in his name, speaks to the daughters of Jerusalem about her sun-darkened appearance and her brothers’ demands, and asks where he pastures his flock; a brief response in verse 4 is assigned to the Friends. Readers in both Arminian and Reformed traditions commonly hold two main approaches side by side: a literal reading that celebrates human love within marriage as a good gift of God, and an allegorical or typological reading that hears the love of God for Israel or of Christ for the church (compare Hosea 2:19–20; Ephesians 5:31–32). Many readers combine the two, and neither approach belongs to one tradition.

verses.text: The Song of songs, which is Solomon’s.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers commonly read the title as presenting the finest of songs, whether written by Solomon, for him, or about him. Many value both a literal reading of marital love and a figurative reading of divine love.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers commonly read the title as marking the Song as a choice part of Scripture, inspired and profitable whatever its authorship. Many likewise hold literal and figurative readings together.

verses.text: Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth; for your love is better than wine.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers who read the Song literally see the Beloved’s longing for her beloved’s affection as an honest expression of love. Figurative readers hear the soul’s desire for communion with God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers who read the Song literally see desire honored within covenant love as a good gift of God. Figurative readers hear the church’s longing for Christ, whose love is better than any earthly delight.

verses.text: Your oils have a pleasing fragrance. Your name is oil poured out, therefore the virgins love you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved praising his good name and the fragrance of his presence. Figurative readers commonly hear the attractiveness of God’s name, which draws many to love him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see reputation and character treasured in love. Figurative readers commonly hear Christ’s name as fragrant and drawing the faithful, an image both traditions share.

verses.text: Take me away with you. Let’s hurry. The king has brought me into his rooms. We will be glad and rejoice in you. We will praise your love more than wine! They are right to love you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved asking to be drawn along, and the Friends, as the WEB labels them, joining in rejoicing. Love is celebrated by the wider community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the shared gladness of the Beloved and the Friends as love that others recognize and honor. Figurative readers commonly hear the joy of God’s people together in his presence.

verses.text: I am dark, but lovely, you daughters of Jerusalem, like Kedar’s tents, like Solomon’s curtains.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved speaking to the daughters of Jerusalem with both candor and confidence about her appearance. She knows she is loved.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a frank self-description held together with a sense of worth. Figurative readers commonly hear the church confessing her flaws while trusting that she is lovely in her Lord’s sight.

verses.text: Don’t stare at me because I am dark, because the sun has scorched me. My mother’s sons were angry with me. They made me keeper of the vineyards. I haven’t kept my own vineyard.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved explaining that work in the sun under her brothers’ demands has kept her from tending her own vineyard. Hardship has shaped her life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see honest acknowledgment of family strain and neglected self-care. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse with sympathy rather than forcing a detailed symbolic meaning.

verses.text: Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you graze your flock, where you rest them at noon; for why should I be as one who is veiled beside the flocks of your companions?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved asking where the one whom her soul loves pastures his flock, so she need not wander. Love seeks the beloved directly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see sincere longing for presence and rest. Figurative readers commonly hear the believer seeking the Good Shepherd and his rest at noon (compare John 10:11; Psalm 23:2).
